title: OET Reading Practice Test 1
instructions: OET Reading has three parts. Part A: rapid reading across short healthcare texts. Part B: short workplace texts. Part C: two longer healthcare texts. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part A — Expeditious Reading
parts.description: Four short texts on a single healthcare topic; locate specific information quickly.

parts.title: Part B — Workplace Texts
parts.description: Short workplace documents (policies, manuals, guidelines, emails); identify the main point or purpose.

parts.title: Part C — Presentation Texts
parts.description: Two longer texts; detailed comprehension of opinion, attitude and meaning.

passages.title: Wound Care Management
passages.text: Proper wound assessment is essential for all healthcare professionals working in acute and community settings. A basic assessment should include wound size, depth, colour, odour, exudate type and drainage. Clean wounds with normal saline and apply appropriate dressings based on wound type. Infected wounds require increased dressing frequency and possible antibiotic therapy. Healthcare workers must report signs of infection such as increased pain, redness, or purulent discharge to the supervising physician immediately. Sterile technique should always be maintained during dressing changes to prevent secondary infection. Documentation of wound progress should occur at every dressing change.

passages.title: Hospital Infection Control Policy
passages.text: Standard Precautions must be applied to all patient care. Hand hygiene is the most effective measure to prevent cross-infection. Healthcare staff must wash hands with soap and water or use alcohol-based hand sanitiser before and after patient contact, and after touching bodily fluids. Personal protective equipment (PPE) including gloves, masks, and gowns should be worn when exposure to blood or bodily fluids is anticipated. Sharps must be disposed of in designated sharps containers immediately after use. All staff must complete annual infection control training and competency checks.

passages.title: Medication Administration Guidelines
passages.text: The five rights of medication administration must be followed: right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, and right time. Always verify patient identity using two forms of identification. Check medication labels three times: when removing from storage, before preparation, and at the bedside. If a dose is missed, do not double the next dose. Document all medications given with patient name, drug name, dose, route, time, and signature. Report any adverse reactions to the prescribing physician within two hours of administration.

passages.title: Falls Prevention in Elderly Patients
passages.text: Falls are a leading cause of hospitalisation in older adults, with serious consequences including hip fractures, head injuries, and loss of independence. Healthcare facilities must implement comprehensive falls prevention programmes. Risk assessment should be performed at admission and regularly thereafter, identifying patients at high risk such as those on sedating medications, with history of falls, or with cognitive impairment. Environmental modifications are crucial: remove trip hazards, ensure adequate lighting, install grab bars in bathrooms, and maintain clear pathways. Staff should encourage use of mobility aids and provide supervision during transfers. Educating patients and families about fall risks and prevention strategies improves outcomes. Research shows that multifactorial interventions—combining assessment, exercise, medication review, and environmental changes—reduce falls by up to 30%. Prompt reporting of falls incidents helps identify system weaknesses and implement targeted improvements.

passages.title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Management
passages.text: COPD is a progressive disease characterised by persistent airflow limitation. Symptoms include chronic cough, dyspnoea, and reduced exercise tolerance. Early diagnosis is vital as smoking cessation can slow disease progression significantly. Spirometry is the gold standard diagnostic test, measuring forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1). Treatment is based on disease severity and symptom burden. Inhaled bronchodilators are first-line therapy, with options including short-acting beta-2 agonists for acute relief and long-acting agents for maintenance. Inhaled corticosteroids are added for moderate to severe disease with frequent exacerbations. Pulmonary rehabilitation programmes combining exercise, education, and psychosocial support improve quality of life and reduce hospital admissions. Patients should receive annual influenza vaccination and pneumococcal vaccination to prevent respiratory infections. Exacerbations, often triggered by infections or air pollution, require intensified treatment and may necessitate hospitalisation. Regular monitoring of lung function and symptom control guides therapy adjustments.
